newsitem.title: USA: FDA seeking power to kill tobacco industry, lawyer asserts.
newsitem.headline: FDA seeking power to kill tobacco industry, lawyer asserts.

text.p: The Food and Drug Administration is seeking powers that ultimately could be used to shut down the tobacco industry in the United States, a lawyer for cigarette companies told a federal court Monday.

"The FDA is asserting power to ban this industry," Richard Cooper, an attorney representing cigarette makers, said as U.S. District Judge William Osteen Sr. opened a one-day hearing in the tobacco industry's suit against the FDA.

"It's not going to exercise that power for now ... but it has expressly reserved this momentous power for the future," Cooper said as tobacco companies pressed their claim that the FDA is trying to control cigarettes unlawfully.
Cooper, a former chief counsel for the FDA, said the federal agency's proposed new regulations of tobacco are "an extraordinary assertion of power."
The judge is expected to be the first to rule on whether the FDA has the right to regulate cigarette sales and marketing and whether the proposed rules are constitutional.

Monday's arguments focused on the tobacco industry's motion for summary judgment in which the judge has been asked to make a decision on the merits of the case without a trial. If Osteen feels he needs additional evidence, he will schedule a trial in the near future.
The judge said he hoped to render a decision within five to 10 weeks.

Since the first set of FDA rules is set to take effect on Feb. 28, lawyers believed that Osteen will either make a ruling in the case by that time or perhaps issue a temporary stay of the regulations until a decision is reached.

"The tobacco regulations mark the first time in the history of the FDA that the agency has asserted jurisdiction over cigarettes and smokeless tobacco products as customarily marketed," the industry said in its motion.

"That assertion of authority overturns FDA's own settled interpretation of food and drug law dating back to 1914, and violates longstanding reliance by Congress and the tobacco sector of the national economy on the established understanding of the limits of FDA's jurisdiction."
Regardless of the outcome, it is expected that Osteen's ruling will be appealed to the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals and most likely to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Battalions of lawyers, tobacco and government officials and reporters began lining up at 6 a.m. to vie for the 200 seats in the federal courthouse here.
Monday's battle dates back to August 1995, when President Bill Clinton authorised the FDA to regulate how cigarettes are sold and marketed in a bid to curb smoking among children.

The FDA rules would ban free samples and billboard ads near schools and playgrounds, limit vending machine sales, ban sponsorship of sports events and the use of cigarette brands on hats, T-shirts and other products.
The rules would restrict advertising in some publications and require retailers to see picture identification for cigarette purchasers under 27 years old.

Virginia, Kentucky and North Carolina, all major tobacco-growing states, have filed court papers urging the court to overturn the regulations. But at least 33 states, along with San Francisco and Guam, are supporting the rules.

The tobacco industry and other plaintiffs will present three main arguments during the hearing. They involve the intent of Congress concerning tobacco regulation, the language and legislative history of the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act and First Amendment issues.
Osteen could use any of the three arguments to invalidate all of the rules.
